claims.text: The government budget is the government's plan, usually set out once a year, of the revenue it expects to raise - most of it from taxation - and the spending it intends to carry out on public services.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Where a government's planned spending exceeds its expected revenue, the budget is in deficit and the gap tends to be covered by borrowing; where expected revenue exceeds planned spending, the budget is in surplus.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A budget deficit and a current account deficit are different balances: the budget deficit compares government spending with government revenue, while the current account deficit compares the value of a country's exports of goods and services with the value of its imports.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A budget that plans N$72 billion of spending against N$64 billion of revenue is in deficit by the N$8 billion that must be borrowed to bridge the gap.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Governments spend to provide goods and services that markets tend to under-provide: public goods such as defence, policing and street lighting, and merit goods such as schooling and clinics.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Governments spend to redistribute income, through pensions and grants that transfer spending power towards households on low incomes.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Where total spending in the economy is weak and workers sit idle, raising government spending tends to raise output and employment where there is spare capacity in the economy; near full capacity, extra spending tends instead to push prices up.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Spending N$500 million on resurfacing a major road employs road crews whose wages are then spent in the towns along the route, sustaining further jobs - a chain from one public project to incomes across the region.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A tax is a compulsory payment to a government, levied on income, spending or wealth, owed whether or not the payer receives any specific service in return.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Governments levy taxes first of all to raise the revenue that pays for public spending.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Governments also levy taxes to redistribute income from higher earners towards households on lower incomes, and to make the price of a demerit good carry more of the harm its use imposes on others.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Direct taxation and indirect taxation are told apart by what the charge falls on and who hands it over: a direct tax is levied on income or profit and paid straight to the revenue authority by the person or firm taxed, while an indirect tax is levied on spending and collected by the seller from the buyer.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Income tax on wages and company tax on profit are direct taxes paid over by the taxed party itself; value-added tax on a shop bill and excise duty on fuel are indirect taxes, collected by traders from buyers and passed on.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A progressive tax takes a rising share of income as income rises; a regressive tax takes a larger share of a low income than of a high one; a proportional tax takes the same share of every income.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: An income tax that takes 15 per cent of a N$10 000 wage but 20 per cent of a N$30 000 wage is progressive, while a value-added tax at a flat rate is regressive in effect, because poorer households spend a larger part of their incomes.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The consequences of an increase in taxes are not its cause: the tax change is the cause, and the changes that follow - lower disposable income, dearer goods, changed buying - are consequences of an increase in taxes; the test is to ask which way the direction of events runs.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Interest rates are not taxes: an interest rate is the price paid for borrowing money, while a tax is a compulsory levy on income or spending; the test is to ask who sets the charge and what it falls on.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The principles of taxation, first set out by Adam Smith, are commonly stated as equity, certainty, convenience and economy.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Equity in taxation means those with a greater ability to pay bear a larger share; certainty means the payer knows what is due, when and how; convenience means payment falls due where and when it is easy to pay; economy means the tax costs little to collect relative to what it raises.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Pay-as-you-earn income tax, deducted from a worker's wage each month by the employer and passed to the revenue authority, shows convenience, certainty and economy together.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A higher income tax lowers workers' disposable income, which tends to reduce their spending on goods and services, and may weaken the incentive to work longer or take untaxed income out of sight.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: An indirect tax added to a good's price raises the price buyers face, and the quantity demanded of the good tends to fall; how much revenue the tax yields depends on how strongly buyers keep buying at the higher price.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Taxes change people's choices: set high, they tend to push buying into untaxed channels - cross-border trips, informal stalls, undeclared cash work - so the quantity falls by less and the revenue raised falls short of the forecast.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Fuel duty of N$3 a litre adds N$150 to a 50-litre tank, a cost a haulage firm must find from fares or margins and that tends to steer passengers towards fewer journeys.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Fiscal policy is the use of government spending, taxation and borrowing to influence the economy.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The measures of fiscal policy are changes in the level of government spending, changes in the rates and structure of taxation, and changes in the amount the government borrows.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: An expansionary fiscal stance raises government spending or cuts tax rates to lift total spending in the economy; a contractionary stance cuts spending or raises tax rates to slow it.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A government sets its fiscal stance through the yearly budget: it forecasts revenue, decides spending plans, and borrows where the two do not balance.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Where there is spare capacity, an increase in government spending tends to raise output and employment; as the economy approaches full capacity, further spending tends to raise the general price level instead.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Fiscal measures may move the macroeconomic aims against one another: a stance that lowers unemployment tends to add pressure to prices, and a stance that steadies prices tends to slow output and jobs.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A budget deficit shifts part of the cost of today's spending onto future taxpayers, who meet the interest and repayments from later budgets; whether it is justified turns on what the borrowed funds buy and on the size of the gap.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The yearly budget is the instrument of fiscal policy: its spending plans and tax decisions together set the fiscal stance for the year ahead.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.
